title: Bryostatin-1 exploits a developmental signaling vulnerability in MEF2D-rearranged B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia
summary: MEF2D-rearranged (MEF2D-r) B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia (BCP-ALL) is a rare molecular subtype associated with high-risk clinical features and frequent relapse and characterized by a distinctive pre-B-cell developmental state and dependence on pre-B-cell receptor (pre-BCR) signaling. Despite these distinctive biological features, MEF2D-r BCP-ALL lacks subtype-directed therapy. Here, we identify a pharmacologically actionable vulnerability to the diacylglycerol (DAG) mimetic bryostatin-1 (Bryo-1). Across 93 BCP-ALL cell lines, MEF2D-r models were enriched for Bryo-1 sensitivity, although responses varied within the subtype and extended to selected non-MEF2D models. Sensitive cells responded at low-nanomolar concentrations with rapid ERK activation followed by loss of pre-BCR-associated components, reduced proliferation, caspase activation and cell death. Pharmacological MEK inhibition markedly attenuated Bryo-1-induced loss of viability, supporting a functional involvement of MEK-ERK signaling. Time-resolved phosphoproteomic and proteomic analyses further revealed coordinated activation of DAG-responsive signaling and subsequent remodeling of the precursor B-cell state. Bryo-1 also altered immunotherapy-relevant surface antigens, including CD19, CD20 and CD22, as part of this broader cell-state transition. Importantly, low-nanomolar activity was reproduced ex vivo in MEF2D-r patient-derived xenograft cells. Together, these findings support pharmacological activation of a negative-selection-like developmental checkpoint as a potential therapeutic strategy in responsive MEF2D-r BCP-ALL and provide a framework for biomarker-guided functional patient selection.

title: High GPX4 Expression Marks an Oxidative-Metabolic, PD-L1/CD47-Low and Stroma-Poor Tumor State in Hepatocellular Carcinoma
summary: Background: Glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) protects cancer cells from ferroptosis and is a candidate therapeutic target in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). How GPX4 expression relates to the immune and metabolic features of patient tumors is not well characterized. Methods: We analyzed RNA-sequencing data from 366 primary tumors of the TCGA-LIHC PanCancer Atlas cohort (365 with survival data). Associations between GPX4 and ten immune and stress-response markers were tested by Spearman correlation with Benjamini-Hochberg correction, then re-estimated after adjustment for consensus tumor purity, CTNNB1 and TP53 mutation, age and sex. A T-cell-inflamed profile, a CD8 T-cell score and an NRF2 target-gene score, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) of GPX4-high versus GPX4-low tumors, and Cox models were added as further tests. Results: Higher GPX4 expression was associated with lower expression of PD-L1 (CD274; rho = -0.34, 95% CI -0.43 to -0.24, p = 2.4 x 10^-11), CD47 (rho = -0.21), the macrophage marker CD163 (rho = -0.17) and a fibroblast/extracellular-matrix score (rho = -0.22). These associations persisted after adjustment (CD274 rho = -0.37 in the fully adjusted model). GSEA showed enrichment of oxidative phosphorylation, mitochondrial, fatty-acid, xenobiotic and glutathione metabolism programs and depletion of extracellular-matrix, TGF-beta and cell-adhesion programs in GPX4-high tumors. GPX4 was not associated with a T-cell-inflamed profile (rho = -0.07), a CD8 T-cell score (rho = -0.03), cytolytic activity (rho = 0.04) or an NRF2 target-gene score (rho = 0.03), although NFE2L2 mRNA was inversely correlated with GPX4 (rho = -0.32). GPX4 expression was not associated with overall survival (stage-adjusted hazard ratio per SD 1.09, 95% CI 0.91-1.29). Conclusions: In TCGA-LIHC, high GPX4 expression marks a metabolically active, PD-L1/CD47-low and matrix-poor tumor state, with no evidence of T-cell exclusion, NRF2 pathway activation or prognostic value. These correlative findings come from a single cohort and require external validation and functional testing. Keywords: hepatocellular carcinoma; ferroptosis; GPX4; PD-L1; CD47; tumor microenvironment; NRF2; gene set enrichment analysis; TCGA

title: Media matters: A resource for understanding the determinants of migratory potential of malignant and non-malignant cells
summary: Cell mobility is critical for homeostatic processes such as wound repair and diseases like cancer metastasis. While the advent of migrastatic and antimetastatic therapies has promise, the identification and translation of pathways important for migratory plasticity into druggable targets approved in clinical trials are considerably lacking. To better understand why, we developed an unbiased high-throughput wound-healing/invasion assay to screen for the migratory potential of >60 non-malignant and malignant cell lines derived from the pancreas, colon, skin, breast, prostate, and lung. The goal of this phenotypic screen was to provide a resource of migration/invasion potential and insight into the differential properties not only between malignant and non-malignant cells but also the various carcinomas. Surprisingly, we found non-malignant epithelial cells of the lung, skin, and pancreas migrated/invaded faster than their malignant counterparts. We observed perturbation of glucose metabolism, via inhibition of glycolysis, restricted the migration of non-malignant but not cancer cells, whereas inhibition of oxidative phosphorylation limited the mobility of malignant more than normal cells of the lung, skin, and pancreas. Short-term acclimation of cancer cells in low-nutrient media, containing low/no serum, low calcium, and physiological concentrations of glucose, increased in vitro migration/invasion and in vivo metastatic potential of lung but not pancreatic carcinomas. Phenotypic and metabolic screens presented here could identify prospective therapeutics not only for cancer metastasis, but also diseases driven by the dysregulation of wound-healing/regeneration.

title: YAP activity sustains mitochondrial adaptation to NAMPT inhibition in triple-negative breast cancer
summary: Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) is an essential metabolic cofactor, and maintenance of NAD+ homeostasis is critical for cancer cell survival. Pharmacological inhibition of nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase (NAMPT), the rate-limiting enzyme of the NAD+ salvage pathway, induces NAD+ depletion and energetic stress, although the development of resistance limits its therapeutic potential. We have previously shown that acquired resistance to NAMPT inhibition in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) cells is associated with extensive metabolic rewiring. Here, we investigated the role of the Hippo pathway effector YAP in the cellular adaptation to NAMPT inhibition. Stable YAP downregulation markedly decreased the sensitivity of MDA-MB-231 cells to the NAMPT inhibitors FK866 and CHS-828, whereas re-expression of constitutively active YAP5SA partially restored sensitivity to FK866. YAP-silenced cells maintained NAD(H) and ATP levels during FK866 exposure and showed reduced oxidative stress and caspase 3/7 activation. Comparative proteomic analysis of YAP-silenced cells and cells with acquired FK866 resistance revealed common alterations in mitochondrial, cell-cycle, and RNA-processing programs. Consistently, YAP downregulation altered the cell-cycle response to FK866 and increased mitochondrial respiration, spare respiratory capacity, and mitochondrial mass. These findings identify YAP as a modulator of the cellular response to NAMPT inhibition and suggest that sustained YAP downregulation contributes to the establishment of an adaptive state characterized by reduced proliferative and biosynthetic programs together with increased mitochondrial capacity.

title: Metabolic priming recruits tumour cells across a mitochondrial vulnerability threshold and sensitizes them to chemotherapy
summary: Intratumour heterogeneity allows a fraction of cancer cells to escape otherwise effective treatment. Here we ask whether metabolic priming can recruit heterogeneous tumour cells into a transient mitochondrial state that is selectively vulnerable to photodynamic damage. Tetramethylrhodamine methyl ester (TMRM) has previously been shown to act as a mitochondria targeted photosensitizer; we exploit its voltage-dependent accumulation and dynamic fluorescence during pulsed illumination to quantify vulnerability in single cells. The response is a reproducible fluorescence excursion, a rise to a maximum followed by a decay, accompanied by reactive oxygen species production. Comparing seventeen descriptors of this excursion against subsequent fate in 195 cells across four arms shows that quantities referenced to each cell's own resting value outperform static intensity. The simple difference Fmax F0 predicts death with held-out areas under the curve of approximately 0.75 to 0.79, whereas resting intensity alone carries little transferable information and time to peak does not discriminate fate in the datasets tested. Metabolic priming with the PKM2 activator TEPP46 or with ethyl pyruvate increases the fraction of responding cells; under TEPP46 almost the whole population enters the responding state. PKM2 abundance is associated with faster entry into that state, and PKM2 is heterogeneous in human skin tumour sections. Four hours of camptothecin shifts the response distribution, increasing the fraction of cells above the untreated median from 50% to 76%, identifying a candidate intervention window. In combination experiments, TMRM photodynamic treatment produced survival below the Bliss-independence expectation with camptothecin or TRAIL, in both treatment orders and across three cell lines; these combination measurements are descriptive and require independent replication. The study therefore identifies a perturbation-revealed mitochondrial vulnerability that can be pharmacologically recruited and followed dynamically at single-cell resolution. It is a proof of concept in cultured cells and human tumour sections and has not been tested in vivo.

title: MASH-in-a-dish reveals fatty acid-driven itaconate crosstalk between Kupffer cells and hepatocytes
summary: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) is driven by interactions between metabolically stressed hepatocytes and non-parenchymal liver cells, leading to hepatocyte injury, inflammation, and fibrosis. Metabolites can mediate intercellular communication, yet their contribution to MASH pathogenesis remains poorly understood, partly because tissue dissociation disrupts the local metabolic environment. To address this challenge, we developed a novel in vitro MASH model, "MASH-in-a-dish", a Transwell co-culture system of mouse hepatocyte-derived organoids (HepOrgs), Kupffer cells (KCs), and hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) in a serum-free, chemically defined liver co-culture medium. MASH-in-a-dish modelled key features of clinical MASH, including steatosis, hepatocyte ballooning, inflammation and fibrosis, and allowed for rapid cell separation and cell type-specific metabolomics and stable-isotope fluxomics analysis. Using MASH-in-a-dish, we identified 21 MASH-associated interactive metabolites originating from 6 metabolic pathways, including the tricarboxylic acid cycle and the urea cycle. As a proof of concept, we further characterized itaconate-mediated intercellular crosstalk. Under MASH conditions, fatty acids replaced glucose to drive carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CTP1A)-dependent itaconate production in KCs. Itaconate exacerbated oxidative stress, steatosis, and hepatocyte injury in lipid-stressed HepOrgs. Inhibiting itaconate production by KC-specific Acod1 knockout in the MASH-in-a-dish system mitigated hepatocyte damage. These findings identify fatty acid-driven itaconate production as a mechanism for lipid stress-induced immunometabolic crosstalk, linking adipose tissue insulin resistance to hepatocyte injury in MASH. In conclusion, our results establish MASH-in-a-dish as a powerful and versatile in vitro platform to investigating cell-cell interactions and metabolite crosstalk in MASH pathogenesis, and identify fatty acid-driven itaconate crosstalk between Kupffer cells and hepatocytes as a novel pathogenic mechanism and a potential therapeutic target in MASH.
